groups.sentence: Instructors redesign or adapt their assignments, assessments and learning outcomes in response to generative AI.
Instructors make assignments personal, local, current or tied to specific course materials and discussions, so generic AI output is less useful.
Instructors design assignments that AI cannot easily complete or that resist AI substitution.
Instructors break large assignments into staged parts such as proposals, outlines, drafts and checkpoints, with feedback along the way.
Instructors assess the learning process, through reflection, process documentation and metacognition, not only the final product.
Instructors design authentic, real-world assessments that require application, analysis and higher-order thinking.
Instructors design assignments that build in AI use, such as critiquing, improving or reflecting on AI output.
Instructors use in-class activities, discussion, group work, peer review, presentations and flipped formats so students show learning in person.
Instructors let students submit work in varied formats such as video, audio, podcasts or multimedia instead of only written text.
Instructors use more frequent, low-stakes assessments and give less weight to a few high-stakes ones.
Instructors require students to cite specific, verifiable sources, including links or DOIs, in their assignments.
Instructors write clear rubrics that reward critical thinking, application and original thought.
Instructors test their assignments in AI tools to see how well AI handles them.
Instructors include AI use or the permitted AI level in the grading rubric and grading criteria.
Instructors may explain the purpose and rationale of assignments to students.
Students may use AI in structured assignment tasks such as revising a draft or critiquing an AI response.
Course-specific assignments have students compare or surpass AI-generated solutions, with guidelines for AI use at each stage.
Students follow assignment-specific rules, such as working in a monitored workspace, sending outlines, and not using AI on final papers.
Instructors use controlled assessment conditions such as timed work, handwriting, in-class exams or randomized questions.
Instructors enforce academic dishonesty policies.
Administrators and departments review learning goals and offer alternative assessment approaches in light of AI.
Instructors periodically revisit and replace assignments that AI handles too easily.
Institutions aim to support assessment practices that stay meaningful despite AI.
Students' AI use is documented and graded, and AI use makes their work harder to evaluate.
